rows=[(7,259,275),(8,820,900),(9,2717,3011),(10,9124,10414),(11,31142,36368)]

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: improving the rate of short quaternary codes correcting insertion, deletion, or substitution errors. Using learned embeddings to guide codebook construction is a creative application of representation learning.

Algorithm 1 uses exact Levenshtein-distance pruning, which guarantees minimum distance at least three independently of embedding accuracy. The construction is clearly described and produces explicit, reusable codebooks.

Table 1 demonstrates consistent improvements over random greedy search, with ten-run statistics and a loss-function ablation. At length 11, the best codebook contains 36,368 codewords and achieves a rate of approximately 68.9%.

The decoding experiments provide encouraging empirical evidence: checking four retrieved candidates yields zero observed failures in 100 million trials at each tested length. The reported speedups over brute-force decoding are substantial.

Synthetic data and a linked source-code repository support reproducibility. The authors acknowledge the missing optimality proof and construction scalability limitations. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The central linear-time decoding claim is insufficiently supported. Logarithmic expected nearest-neighbor query time requires assumptions that are not established for these 64-dimensional embeddings. Figure 5 shows runtime increasing from 6 to 367 seconds as length increases from 7 to 11. Moreover, the single-candidate decoder fails on approximately 0.3–0.9% of trials, while the reliable multiple-candidate configuration incurs quadratic verification cost under the paper's own analysis.

The baselines do not establish the necessity or competitiveness of the learned approach. Construction is compared primarily against random selection and asymptotic redundancy expressions, without stronger finite-length greedy or minimum-degree heuristics. Decoding is compared only against scanning the codebook; enumerating single-edit neighbors and checking dictionary membership is an obvious exact alternative. The cited hardness of unrestricted edit distance does not establish hardness in this bounded-distance setting. Classical greedy packing also needs clearer treatment in the novelty discussion.

The justification for the selection criterion contains an incorrect premise: batch normalization does not make embeddings multivariate Gaussian. Neither Gaussian density nor the fixed Mahalanobis score is shown to predict the number of conflicting candidates remaining during search. The binary t-SNE visualization does not validate these relationships, and greedy selection does not generally maximize final codebook size.

The repeated optimality claims exceed the evidence. Matching a proposed redundancy curve provides no certificate of proximity to the largest achievable codebook. At length 11, the reported redundancy is approximately 6.85 bits, while the substitution sphere-packing lower bound is approximately 5.09 bits, leaving substantial uncertainty. Stronger finite-length bounds or certified small-instance comparisons would make this claim assessable.

The practical significance remains incompletely demonstrated. At length 11, the 16.8% codebook-size improvement over random search corresponds to approximately one percentage point of code rate. Experiments concern isolated segments with exactly one edit; synchronization between segments and outer-code overhead are not evaluated, leaving the motivating storage-density benefit unquantified.

Despite the repository link, the manuscript omits important experimental details, including training-pair sampling, optimizer and training schedule, handling of variable-length corrupted inputs, and timing hardware. Construction time and peak memory are also unreported despite enumeration of all 4^n candidates. These omissions limit assessment of reproducibility and practical cost.
